plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 1.1.7
plan.contextChunk: This figure contains three panels, (a), (b), and (c), illustrating the approximation of the area under a curve by inscribed rectangles. Panel (a): a smooth curve over the interval [a, b] with the entire region between the curve and the x-axis shaded. Panel (b): the same curve with a small number of wide rectangles inscribed under it, giving a coarse Riemann sum approximation. Panel (c): the same curve with many narrow rectangles filling most of the gap, giving a much closer approximation to the true area. The figure introduces the Riemann sum approach to defining the definite integral as the limit of rectangular area approximations as the number of rectangles increases without bound.

interactionPlan.concept: The definite integral of a curve over [a, b] is defined as the limit of Riemann sums: as the number of inscribed rectangles increases, their total area converges to the exact area under the curve.
elements: x-axis and y-axis with arrowheads, labeled x and y
smooth wavy blue curve rising from before a, peaking, dipping near the middle, and rising again past b
tick marks and italic labels a and b on the x-axis marking the interval
vertical boundary lines at x = a and x = b from the axis up to the curve
n inscribed rectangles under the curve (light blue fill, dark outlines), each touching the curve with its top-right corner, drawn over [a, b]
shaded region between the curve and the x-axis (continuous light blue fill) shown when n = 0 / exact-area view
text readout of the running Riemann sum approximation and the exact area for comparison

interactions.label: Number of rectangles n
interactions.teaches: Increasing n makes the rectangle tops track the curve ever more closely, so the sum of rectangle areas converges to the exact area under the curve — the Riemann sum approaches the definite integral as n grows without bound

demo_steps.title: The exact area
demo_steps.narration: Set n = 0 to see the goal: the continuously shaded region between the curve and the x-axis over [a, b], whose area we want to define and compute.

demo_steps.title: Coarse approximation
demo_steps.narration: With only 5 wide inscribed rectangles, the approximation misses large gaps near the peak and the valley — the Riemann sum visibly underestimates the true area.

demo_steps.title: Refining the fit
demo_steps.narration: Around n = 15 the gaps shrink dramatically; the rectangle skyline hugs the curve and the running sum closes in on the exact area.

demo_steps.title: Approaching the limit
demo_steps.narration: At n = 40 the rectangles are nearly indistinguishable from the shaded region itself — this is the limit process that defines the definite integral.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The exact area under a curve is not computed directly but is defined as the limit of rectangular approximations as the number of rectangles grows without bound.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single animated panel (per the author's request to merge the three textbook panels into one view): one set of axes, one blue curve with a single peak and a shallow valley over [a, b]. Curve drawn as a smooth cubic-like stroke in medium blue; rectangles filled light blue with thin dark outlines, heights set by right endpoints (inscribed look). a and b labeled in italic serif beneath the axis with vertical boundary lines up to the curve. At n = 0 show the continuous shaded region exactly as panel (a). Rectangle count changes should animate smoothly (bars growing/splitting) rather than popping. A compact readout above or beside the plot shows the current Riemann sum and, for contrast, the exact area, with the gap value highlighted. Overall style matches the textbook: white background, black axes, italic serif axis labels.

Panel (a): a smooth curve over the interval [a, b] with the entire region between the curve and the x-axis shaded. authoredContext: However, for regions with curved boundaries, such as that in Figure 1.1.7a, a more general approach is needed. One such approach is to begin by approximating the area of the region by inscribing a number of rectangles of equal width under the curve and adding the areas of these rectangles (Figure 1.1.7b). Intuition suggests that if we repeat that approximation process using more and more rectangles, then the rectangles will tend to fill in the gaps under the curve, and the approximations will get closer and closer to the exact area under the curve (Figure 1.1.7c). This suggests that we can define the area under the curve to be the limiting value of these approximations. This idea will be considered in detail later, but the point to note here is that once again the concept of a limit comes into play.

discrepancies: the source is a three-panel side-by-side figure (exact area → 5 rectangles → many rectangles) whose didactic point is simultaneous comparison; the generated figure collapses this into one panel, so panels (b) and (c) exist only behind the slider/step player and can never be compared at a glance
rectangle outlines are drawn in blue-gray (#3f738f) instead of the thin black/dark outlines used in source panels (b) and (c)
the curve's peak and valley sit slightly closer to the endpoints a and b than in the source, where the peak is roughly a third of the way across [a, b] and the valley about three-quarters
the 'x' axis label is placed immediately beside the arrowhead tip, slightly crowding it
evaluation.notes: The default n=0 state is a faithful stand-in for source panel (a) — correct curve shape, light-blue fill, arrowed axes, and italic a/b/x/y labels — and the slider plus 4-step player accurately reproduces panels (b) and (c) as right-endpoint Riemann sums with a live sum-vs-exact-gap readout; the only real loss is the source's simultaneous three-panel comparison.
action_items: Change the rectangle stroke color from '#3f738f' to black (or near-black) to match the thin dark rectangle outlines in source panels (b) and (c).
Nudge f(x)'s phase/frequency so the peak falls near one-third and the valley near three-quarters of [a, b], matching the source curve's proportions more closely.
Shift the 'x' label a few pixels right/down so it clears the x-axis arrowhead.
plan_action_items: Consider a synchronized small-multiple option (e.g. a toggle showing the n=0, n=5, and large-n views side by side) so the source's signature side-by-side comparison of refinement stages is preserved alongside the slider.
